## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Read and write regular expressions with character classes, quantifiers and anchors.
2. Escape special characters, and know why R needs two backslashes.
3. Capture parts of a match with groups and pull them out with `str_match()`.
4. Use regular expressions to validate, extract, replace and split text in a data frame.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
```

## What a regular expression is

A **regular expression** (regex) is a short description of a text pattern. On Day 11 you searched for fixed words such as `"Camp"`. A regex can describe "a capital letter followed by digits" or "a word at the end of the line".

`str_view()` shows each match between `<` and `>`. Use it to test a pattern before you rely on it:

```{webr}
ids <- c("HH001", "hh002", "HH 003", "HH0004", "Household 5", "HH00X")
str_view(ids, "HH")
```

Most letters and digits match themselves. A few characters have special meanings. They are what make regex powerful.

## Character classes: which characters

A **character class** matches one character from a set.

| Pattern | Matches one… |
|---|---|
| `.` | of any character |
| `[abc]` | of `a`, `b` or `c` |
| `[a-z]` | lower-case letter |
| `[A-Z0-9]` | capital letter or digit |
| `[^0-9]` | character that is **not** a digit |
| `\\d` | digit (same as `[0-9]`) |
| `\\s` | space, tab or line break |
| `\\w` | letter, digit or underscore |
| `\\D`, `\\S`, `\\W` | the opposite of the three above |

```{webr}
str_view(ids, "\\d")      # every digit
str_view(ids, "[A-Z]")    # every capital letter
str_view(ids, "\\s")      # the space in "HH 003" and "Household 5"
```

## Quantifiers: how many

A **quantifier** comes after a character or class and says how many times it may repeat.

| Quantifier | Means |
|---|---|
| `?` | 0 or 1 times (optional) |
| `+` | 1 or more times |
| `*` | 0 or more times |
| `{3}` | exactly 3 times |
| `{2,4}` | 2 to 4 times |
| `{2,}` | 2 or more times |

```{webr}
str_extract(ids, "\\d+")      # one or more digits
str_extract(ids, "\\d{3}")    # exactly three digits
str_view(c("colour", "color"), "colou?r")   # the u is optional
```

## Anchors: where

**Anchors** match a position, not a character. `^` means the start of the text and `$` means the end.

```{webr}
str_detect(ids, "^HH")         # starts with HH
str_detect(ids, "\\d$")        # ends with a digit
str_detect(ids, "^HH\\d{3}$")  # the whole value is HH and exactly three digits
```

The last pattern is a **validation rule**. Without `^` and `$`, `"HH0004"` would pass, because it *contains* `HH000`. Anchor both ends when you check that a whole value has the right format.

`\\b` is a word boundary. It stops `"camp"` from matching inside `"campaign"`:

```{webr}
notes <- c("near the camp", "campaign office", "Camp B")
str_detect(notes, "camp")
str_detect(notes, regex("\\bcamp\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))
```

`regex(..., ignore_case = TRUE)` makes the match ignore case.

## Escaping: matching special characters

To match a character that has a special meaning, such as `.`, `+`, `(` or `$`, put a backslash in front of it. In an R string, a backslash itself must be written twice. So the regex `\.` ("a real full stop") is typed `"\\."` in R:

```{webr}
amounts <- c("1.5", "15", "2.75")
str_detect(amounts, ".")     # . means any character, so every value matches
str_detect(amounts, "\\.")   # a real full stop
str_replace_all("Price: $25 (approx.)", "[$()]", "")   # inside [ ], most special characters are literal
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why two backslashes?
R reads the string first and treats `\` as the start of an escape, as in `"\n"` for a new line. `"\\d"` becomes the two characters `\d`, which the regex engine then reads as "a digit". If a pattern with backslashes looks hard to read, test it with `str_view()`.
:::

## Alternation and groups

`|` means "or". Brackets `( )` make a **group**, which keeps the alternatives together:

```{webr}
str_detect(c("Gulu", "Arua", "Mbale"), "^(Gulu|Arua)$")
str_view("grey and gray", "gr(e|a)y")
```

Groups also **capture** what they match. `str_match()` returns the whole match in the first column and each group in the next columns:

```{webr}
phones <- c("+256 772 123456", "0772-123456", "256701987654", "call 0414 345678")
str_match(phones, "(\\d{3})[ -]?(\\d{6})$")
```

You can reuse a captured group in a replacement with `\\1`, `\\2` and so on. This reorders day-first dates to year-month-day:

```{webr}
str_replace("15/03/2026", "(\\d{2})/(\\d{2})/(\\d{4})", "\\3-\\2-\\1")
```

## Regex in a data frame

These are the stringr functions you will use most. Each takes the text first and the pattern second.

| Function | Does |
|---|---|
| `str_detect()` | `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each value |
| `str_count()` | how many matches in each value |
| `str_extract()` | the first match |
| `str_extract_all()` | every match, as a list |
| `str_match()` | the match and its groups, as a matrix |
| `str_replace()` / `str_replace_all()` | replace the first or every match |
| `str_remove_all()` | delete every match |
| `str_split()` | split at each match |

Here is a messy free-text column from a field form:

```{webr}
forms <- data.frame(
  id    = c("hh-1", "HH 02", "HH003", "hh_4"),
  notes = c("Paid UGX 25,000 on 03/03/2026", "No payment", "Paid ugx 7,500 on 11/03/2026", "Paid UGX 120,000 on 20/03/2026; follow up")
)

clean <- forms |>
  mutate(
    number = str_extract(id, "\\d+"),
    id     = str_c("HH", str_pad(number, width = 3, pad = "0")),
    paid   = str_detect(notes, regex("^paid", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    amount = notes |> str_extract("[\\d,]+(?= on)") |> str_remove_all(",") |> as.numeric(),
    date   = str_extract(notes, "\\d{2}/\\d{2}/\\d{4}")
  ) |>
  select(-number)
clean
```

`(?= on)` is a **lookahead**: it says "followed by ` on`" without including ` on` in the match. You will not need lookarounds often, but they are handy when the text around a value is the only thing that identifies it.

tidyr has regex helpers too. `separate_wider_regex()` splits one column into several using named patterns:

```{webr}
codes <- data.frame(code = c("GUL-2026-014", "ARU-2025-003"))
codes |>
  separate_wider_regex(code, patterns = c(district = "[A-Z]{3}", "-", year = "\\d{4}", "-", number = "\\d+"))
```

Unnamed pieces, such as `"-"`, are matched and dropped.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Build patterns step by step
Start with a small piece, check it with `str_view()`, then add the next piece. A long regex written in one go is almost always wrong somewhere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
Excel's Find and Replace supports only `*` and `?` as wildcards. Newer versions of Excel have `REGEXTEST()`, `REGEXEXTRACT()` and `REGEXREPLACE()`, which match `str_detect()`, `str_extract()` and `str_replace()`.
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: Validate an ID format

A valid household ID is `HH` followed by **exactly three digits** and nothing else. Use `str_detect()` with a regular expression to mark each ID as valid or not. Save the result as `valid`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_validate
#| setup: true
library(stringr)
ids <- c("HH001", "hh002", "HH 003", "HH0004", "HH12", "HH999")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_validate
valid <- str_detect(ids, "______")
valid
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex13_validate"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Anchor both ends: `^` at the start and `$` at the end. Three digits is `\\d{3}`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex13_validate"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
valid <- str_detect(ids, "^HH\\d{3}$")
valid
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_validate
#| check: true
expected <- c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)
if (!exists("valid") || !is.logical(valid)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "valid should be TRUE or FALSE for each ID. Use str_detect().")
} else if (identical(valid, expected)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Only HH001 and HH999 have the right format.")
} else if (isTRUE(valid[4])) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "HH0004 should be invalid. Add ^ and $ so the whole value must match.")
} else if (isTRUE(valid[2])) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "hh002 should be invalid: the pattern is case-sensitive, so use capital HH.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Try ^HH\\\\d{3}$: HH, then exactly three digits, then the end.")
}
```

### Exercise 2: Extract numbers

Each note contains one amount, written with commas, such as `"25,000"`. Extract the amount, remove the commas and convert it to a number. Save the result as `amounts`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_extract
#| setup: true
library(stringr)
notes <- c("Paid UGX 25,000 in cash", "Transfer of 7,500", "UGX 120,000 by mobile money")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_extract
amounts <- notes |>
  str_extract("______") |>
  str_remove_all(",") |>
  as.numeric()
amounts
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex13_extract"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The amount is one or more characters that are each a digit or a comma: `[\\d,]+`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex13_extract"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
amounts <- notes |>
  str_extract("[\\d,]+") |>
  str_remove_all(",") |>
  as.numeric()
amounts
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_extract
#| check: true
if (!exists("amounts") || !is.numeric(amounts)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "amounts should be numeric. Finish with as.numeric().")
} else if (identical(amounts, c(25000, 7500, 120000))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct.")
} else if (identical(amounts, c(25, 7, 120))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The pattern stops at the comma. Allow commas too: [\\\\d,]+")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Expected 25000, 7500 and 120000. Check the pattern with str_view().")
}
```

### Exercise 3: Clean phone numbers

Phone numbers were typed in many ways. Remove **every character that is not a digit**, then keep only the **last nine digits**. Save the result as `phones_clean`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_phones
#| setup: true
library(stringr)
phones <- c("+256 772 123456", "0772-123456", "(0)701 987 654", "256-414-345678")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_phones
phones_clean <- phones |>
  str_remove_all("______") |>
  str_extract("______")
phones_clean
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex13_phones"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
"Not a digit" is `[^0-9]` or `\\D`. "The last nine digits" is `\\d{9}$`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex13_phones"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
phones_clean <- phones |>
  str_remove_all("\\D") |>
  str_extract("\\d{9}$")
phones_clean
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_phones
#| check: true
expected <- c("772123456", "772123456", "701987654", "414345678")
if (!exists("phones_clean")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save the result as phones_clean.")
} else if (identical(phones_clean, expected)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Four spellings, one format.")
} else if (any(str_detect(phones_clean, "\\D"), na.rm = TRUE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Some values still contain spaces or symbols. Remove everything that is not a digit with \\\\D.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Keep only the last nine digits with \\\\d{9}$.")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Reorder with groups

Turn day-first dates such as `"15/03/2026"` into year-month-day text such as `"2026-03-15"`, using `str_replace()` with three capture groups and `\\1`, `\\2` and `\\3` in the replacement. Save the result as `iso`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_groups
#| setup: true
library(stringr)
dates <- c("15/03/2026", "02/04/2026", "28/02/2025")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_groups
iso <- str_replace(dates, "(\\d{2})/(\\d{2})/(\\d{4})", "______")
iso
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex13_groups"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Group 1 is the day, group 2 the month and group 3 the year. The replacement is `"\\3-\\2-\\1"`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex13_groups"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
iso <- str_replace(dates, "(\\d{2})/(\\d{2})/(\\d{4})", "\\3-\\2-\\1")
iso
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_groups
#| check: true
if (!exists("iso")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save the result as iso.")
} else if (identical(iso, c("2026-03-15", "2026-04-02", "2025-02-28"))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. as.Date(iso) would now work directly.")
} else if (identical(iso, c("2026-15-03", "2026-02-04", "2025-28-02"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Day and month are swapped. The order is year, month, day: \\\\3-\\\\2-\\\\1.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use \\\\3 for the year, \\\\2 for the month and \\\\1 for the day, separated by dashes.")
}
```

### Exercise 5: Extract parts in a data frame

The `code` column has the form `district-year-number`, such as `"GUL-2026-014"`. Add a column `district` with the three capital letters and a column `year` with the four-digit year **as a number**. Save the result as `sites2`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_df
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
sites <- data.frame(code = c("GUL-2026-014", "ARU-2025-003", "MBA-2026-101"))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_df
sites2 <- sites |>
  mutate(
    district = str_extract(code, "______"),
    year     = as.numeric(str_extract(code, "______"))
  )
sites2
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex13_df"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The district is three capital letters at the start: `^[A-Z]{3}`. The year is exactly four digits: `\\d{4}`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex13_df"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
sites2 <- sites |>
  mutate(
    district = str_extract(code, "^[A-Z]{3}"),
    year     = as.numeric(str_extract(code, "\\d{4}"))
  )
sites2
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex13_df
#| check: true
if (!exists("sites2") || !all(c("district", "year") %in% names(sites2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "sites2 needs the columns district and year.")
} else if (!identical(sites2$district, c("GUL", "ARU", "MBA"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "district should be GUL, ARU and MBA. Use ^[A-Z]{3}.")
} else if (!is.numeric(sites2$year)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "year should be a number. Wrap str_extract() in as.numeric().")
} else if (identical(sites2$year, c(2026, 2025, 2026))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "year should be 2026, 2025 and 2026. Use \\\\d{4} for exactly four digits.")
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **One backslash.** `"\d"` is an error in R. Write `"\\d"`.
- **Forgetting anchors in validation.** `str_detect(x, "\\d{3}")` is `TRUE` for `"12345"`. Use `^\\d{3}$` to check the whole value.
- **Using `.` to mean a full stop.** `.` matches any character. Escape it: `"\\."`.
- **Greedy matches.** `.*` takes as much as it can. `str_extract("<a><b>", "<.*>")` returns `"<a><b>"`, not `"<a>"`. Add `?` to make it take as little as possible: `"<.*?>"`.
- **Case.** Patterns are case-sensitive. Use `regex(pattern, ignore_case = TRUE)` or clean the case first.

## Summary

- A regex describes a pattern. Test it with `str_view()`.
- Character classes (`[a-z]`, `\\d`, `\\s`, `\\w`) say which characters, quantifiers (`?`, `+`, `*`, `{n}`) say how many, and anchors (`^`, `$`, `\\b`) say where.
- Escape special characters with `\\`. In R, every regex backslash is written twice.
- `|` means "or". Groups `( )` capture parts of a match for `str_match()` and for `\\1` in replacements.
- Use regex with `str_detect()`, `str_extract()`, `str_replace_all()`, `str_remove_all()` and tidyr's `separate_wider_regex()`.
